title: Bash Script 2 — Loops, Functions, Pitfalls
lead: Do not do the same work a hundred times: build loops, case and functions, clean up temporary files with trap and write safe scripts without quoting traps.
objectives: You write repeated work with `for` and `while`.
You read a file safely line by line with `while IFS= read -r`.
You route arguments and menus with `case` and structure code with functions and `local`.
You clean up with `mktemp` and `trap` and prevent the empty-variable disaster with `"${DIR:?}"`.
You find script errors with `shellcheck`, `bash -n` and `bash -x`.

sections.title: Loops: for and while
body: A script is more than commands running in order. If you do the same work for several servers or files, you use a **loop**. `for` runs once per item in a list, `while` runs as long as a condition stays true.
The source of the list must be safe: file patterns (`./*.txt`), fixed lists or `"$@"`. Never feed the output of `$(ls)` into a loop; names with spaces get split.
**Note:** The built-in simulator cannot execute loops; you write them into script files and run them in your VM.

commands.what: Runs the commands once for each item in the list.
commands.where: When running the same check on several servers or processing the files of a folder.
commands.why: Shortens repeated code and reduces mistakes.
commands.example: for i in 1 2 3; do echo "n=$i"; done

commands.what: Repeats the commands as long as the condition is true.
commands.where: When waiting for something or reading files.
commands.why: You do not need to know the number of rounds in advance.

commands.what: Brace expansion: produces 1 2 3 4 5 (no spaces inside the range).
commands.where: For number ranges or numbered series of files.
commands.why: Makes short lists without a loop; also used in `for i in {1..5}`.

commands.what: `break` ends the loop, `continue` jumps to the next round.
commands.where: When skipping empty lines or leaving once the item is found.
commands.why: Avoids needless work and nested `if` blocks.

sections.tip: If a file pattern matches nothing, `./*.txt` stays literal. Put `[ -e "$f" ] || continue` at the start of the loop body.

sections.title: Reading a file line by line
body: The correct pattern for line-by-line reading is `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < file`. `IFS=` keeps leading and trailing spaces, `-r` does not interpret backslashes.
Do not write `for line in $(cat file)`: lines are split at spaces and every word becomes a round. The redirection `done < ~/lab/servers.txt` makes the file the input of the loop.

commands.what: Reads input line by line and puts each line into a variable.
commands.where: With server lists, logs or CSV files.
commands.why: Reads safely without altering spaces or backslashes.
commands.example: while IFS= read -r host; do echo "$host"; done < servers.txt

commands.what: Redirects the loop's input from a file.
commands.where: On the last line of a `while read` block.
commands.why: A pipe (`cat | while`) runs in a subshell and variables vanish after the loop; a redirection does not.

commands.what: Prints the number of lines.
commands.where: When you want to know how many rounds the loop will run.
commands.why: You compare your expectation with the real number.

sections.warn: If the last line does not end with `\n`, `read` may skip it. If needed, add `|| [ -n "$host" ]`.

sections.title: Branching with case
body: `case` compares a value with patterns and is far more readable than a long `if/elif` chain. Each branch starts with `pattern)` and ends with `;;`; `*)` runs when nothing matches. The block closes with `esac`.
Typical uses: branching on the first argument (`$1`) as in `./menu.sh start`, or acting differently by the prefix of a server name.

commands.what: Branches a value according to patterns.
commands.where: In service scripts (start/stop/status) and menus.
commands.why: Readable; you catch unknown input with `*)`.
commands.example: case "$1" in start) echo go ;; *) echo usage ;; esac

commands.what: First argument, all arguments and the number of arguments.
commands.where: When passing values to the script from outside.
commands.why: The script becomes reusable; `"$@"` preserves arguments with spaces.

commands.what: Gives the script execute permission.
commands.where: Before running it as `./menu.sh`.
commands.why: Without the permission you get `Permission denied`.

sections.tip: Combine several patterns with `|`, for example `start|restart)`.

sections.title: Functions, local and arrays
body: A **function** names repeated code: `name() { ...; }`. In Bash variables are **global** by default; without `local` inside a function you overwrite variables from outside.

`return` only gives an exit code of 0–255. For text use `echo` and capture it with `$(function)`. An **array** collects several values under one name; always write `"${arr[@]}"` in loops so elements with spaces stay intact.

commands.what: Gives a block of code a name that you call later.
commands.where: When the same check runs in several places in the script.
commands.why: Structures the code, ends repetition and makes testing easier.

commands.what: Limits a variable to the function.
commands.where: For temporary variables inside functions.
commands.why: You do not accidentally overwrite a variable of the same name outside.

commands.what: Defines an array with three elements.
commands.where: For lists of servers or options.
commands.why: The list lives in one variable; `${#arr[@]}` gives the count.

commands.what: Expands each element as a separate quoted word.
commands.where: When building a `for` loop over an array.
commands.why: Elements with spaces are not split.
commands.example: for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do echo "$h"; done

sections.tip: Arrays exist only in Bash, not in `sh` (dash). Put `#!/usr/bin/env bash` on the first line.

sections.title: Safe scripts: set, mktemp, trap
body: Create temporary files not with a fixed name but with `mktemp`: the name is unique and unpredictable. With `trap ... EXIT` the cleanup function runs however the script ends (error, Ctrl+C, normal); `kill -9` is the exception.
`set -euo pipefail` makes the script stricter: stop on errors (`-e`), stop on undefined variables (`-u`), do not hide failures inside pipelines (`pipefail`).

commands.what: Creates a temporary directory with a unique name and prints its path.
commands.where: When the script needs intermediate files.
commands.why: Prevents collisions and attacks through predictable names.

commands.what: Runs the `cleanup` function when the script ends.
commands.where: With temporary directories, lock files or connections.
commands.why: Everything is cleaned up even after an error.

commands.what: Stops the script on errors, undefined variables and pipeline failures.
commands.where: In the first lines of the script.
commands.why: You stop at once instead of silently continuing wrongly.

sections.danger: If you delete inside `trap`, the same rule applies: write `rm -rf "${tmp:?}"`. If `tmp` is empty, `rm -rf $tmp/` really becomes `rm -rf /`. Test first with `echo rm -rf "$tmp"`.

sections.title: Pitfalls and debugging
body: The most common mistake is the **unquoted variable**: `touch $F` with `F="my notes.txt"` creates two files (`my` and `notes.txt`). Rule: always quote variables as `"$F"`.

The most dangerous line is `rm -rf $DIR/*`: if `DIR` is empty it becomes `rm -rf /*`. `"${DIR:?}"` stops the script with an error on an empty or undefined value. Show the path with `echo` before deleting.
Debugging: `bash -n` checks the syntax without running, `bash -x` shows every command with a `+` prefix, `shellcheck` finds common traps.

commands.what: Quotes the variable; no word splitting and no glob expansion.
commands.where: Every time you use a variable.
commands.why: File names with spaces stay in one piece.

commands.what: Aborts with an error if `DIR` is empty or undefined.
commands.where: With `rm -rf` and other destructive commands.
commands.why: Prevents an empty variable from deleting the path `/`.

commands.what: Statically analyses the script and reports traps with a code (SC2086).
commands.where: After writing a script, before committing.
commands.why: Catches unquoted variables and similar mistakes without running anything.

commands.what: Checks only the syntax without running the script.
commands.where: When you suspect a missing `done`, `fi` or `esac`.
commands.why: Harmless; no command runs.

commands.what: Prints every command with its expansions and a `+` prefix.
commands.where: When the script behaves unexpectedly.
commands.why: You see what the variables really contain.

sections.tip: Run a destructive command first with `echo` in front: `echo rm -rf "$DIR"`. If the output is right, remove the `echo`.
sections.warn: Install ShellCheck on Ubuntu/Debian with `sudo apt install shellcheck`, on Rocky/Alma via EPEL: `sudo dnf install epel-release`, then `sudo dnf install ShellCheck`.

t01.text: Create `~/scripts/loop.sh` with `printf`; its first line should be `#!/usr/bin/env bash` (redirection `>`).
t01.hint: `printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\n' > ~/scripts/loop.sh` — the `\n` at the end is the line break.

t02.text: How many servers are in `~/lab/servers.txt`? Count with `wc -l` and guess how many rounds a loop would run.

t03.text: Append with `>>` (without overwriting) a `for i in 1 2 3; do ... done` loop to `loop.sh`: three lines with `printf`.
t03.hint: Inside single quotes the shell does not expand `$i`. Use `\n` for line breaks.

t05.text: Write `~/scripts/readlines.sh` using the pattern `while IFS= read -r host; do ... done < ~/lab/servers.txt` that prints every server with `echo`.
t05.hint: Write four lines with a single `printf`; the last line is `done < ~/lab/servers.txt`.

t06.text: Set `F="my notes.txt"` and create the file with `touch "$F"`. What would have happened without quotes?
t06.hint: Two commands: first the assignment, then `touch "$F"`. Check with `ls`.

t07.text: Write `~/scripts/arr.sh`: it defines the array `hosts=(web01 web02 db01)` and prints it with `for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do ... done`.
t07.hint: Inside the single-quoted `printf`, `"${hosts[@]}"` is written as is.

t08.text: Guess the output of `./scripts/count.sh | wc -l` before running it: how many lines? Then run it and verify.
t08.hint: The script contains three `echo` lines; look with `cat scripts/count.sh`.

t09.text: Set an empty variable with `DIR=` and run `echo "rm -rf $DIR/"`. Which path would it delete? Guess, then verify.
t09.hint: The empty `$DIR` vanishes; only `/` remains. That is why you write `"${DIR:?}"`.

t10.text: `~/scripts/hello.sh` does not run (`Permission denied`). Fix it and run it.
t10.hint: `ls -l ~/scripts` shows the permissions; `chmod +x` adds them; then `~/scripts/hello.sh`.

t11.text: The line `rm -rf $DIR/*` in `~/scripts/clean.sh` is dangerous. Rewrite the file: keep `DIR=/home/student/tmpwork`, and make the delete line use `"${DIR:?}/"*`.
t11.hint: Look with `cat ~/scripts/clean.sh`; then rewrite the three lines with `printf`.

t12.text: `~/scripts/list_files.sh` contains `for f in $(ls *.txt)`, which splits names with spaces. Rewrite the file with a glob: `for f in ./*.txt; do`.
t12.hint: Look at the content with `cat`. Rewrite four lines with `printf`; keep `$f` inside single quotes.

t13.text: Create `~/scripts/menu.sh`: `case "$1" in` with branches `start)`, `stop)` and `*)`, ending with `esac`; then make it executable.
t13.hint: Write the file with one `printf`, then `chmod 755`. Every branch ends with `;;`.

t14.text: Write `~/scripts/safe.sh`: a temp directory with `mktemp -d`, a `cleanup()` function, `trap cleanup EXIT` and a `log()` function that uses `local`.
t14.hint: First `tmp=$(mktemp -d)`, then `cleanup() { rm -rf "${tmp:?}"; }`, and `trap cleanup EXIT` at the end.

t15.text: Which servers logged an `ERROR` in `~/lab/app.log`? Write the unique, sorted server names to `~/lab/failed_hosts.txt`.
t15.hint: `grep ERROR`, then `cut -d' ' -f4`, `sort -u`; redirect the output with `>` into the file.

t16.text: Ticket: The nightly cleanup script deleted more than expected on a server because the variable was empty. Write `~/scripts/cleanup.sh`: `set -euo pipefail`, `DIR=/home/student/tmpwork`, a `trap` on exit, `"${DIR:?}/"*` for deleting; make it executable.
t16.hint: One `printf` with five lines, then `chmod 755`. `trap "echo cleanup done" EXIT` is enough.

t17.text: Ticket: The team wants a script that checks every server in `~/lab/servers.txt`. Write `~/scripts/check_all.sh`: a `check_host()` function using `local`, a `while IFS= read -r host; do` loop, `done < ~/lab/servers.txt`; make it executable.
t17.hint: Function first, then the loop; skip blank lines with `[ -n "$host" ] || continue`; `chmod 755` last.

vm.intro: Do these tasks in your own VM (Ubuntu, Rocky/Alma or WSL). Everything happens under `~/scripts`; do not touch system files. Before trying anything with `rm`, take a VM snapshot (Module 0.2) and put `echo` in front of the delete command.

v01.title: First loop and bash -n
v01.text: Write a `for` loop, check it first with `bash -n`, then run it. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/scripts && cd ~/scripts
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash
for i in 1 2 3; do
  echo "n=$i"
done
' > loop.sh
chmod +x loop.sh
bash -n loop.sh && ./loop.sh

differs: If `bash -n` reports an error, check the `do` and `done` lines with `cat loop.sh`.
If you see `Permission denied`, you forgot `chmod +x loop.sh`.

v02.title: Loop over a file and case
v02.text: Read the server list line by line and print a role with `case` according to each name.

blocks.expected:
web01: web
web02: web
db01: database
cache01: other
mail01: other

differs: If the output is empty, check with `ls` that `servers.txt` is in the same folder.
If everything says `other`, you have a typo in the `case` patterns (`web*)`).

v03.title: Function, local, mktemp, trap
v03.text: Run a script that creates a temporary directory and cleans it up on exit. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/scripts
cat > safe.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() {
  rm -rf "${tmp:?}"
  echo "cleanup: removed $tmp"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
log() {
  local msg=$1
  echo "work in $tmp: $msg"
}
log "hello"
EOF
bash safe.sh

differs: The directory name differs on every run; what matters is that both lines appear.
If the `cleanup` line is missing, check that `trap cleanup EXIT` comes after the function.

v04.title: Catching traps with shellcheck
v04.text: Install ShellCheck and scan a script that has an unquoted variable. Paste the warning.

blocks.cmd:
# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt install -y shellcheck
# Rocky/Alma (needs EPEL)
sudo dnf install -y epel-release && sudo dnf install -y ShellCheck

cd ~/scripts
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash
F="my notes.txt"
touch $F
' > bad.sh
shellcheck bad.sh
blocks.expected:
In bad.sh line 3:
touch $F
      ^-- SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.

differs: If the install fails, on Rocky check with `dnf repolist` that `epel-release` is active.
The message differs slightly between ShellCheck versions; the code `SC2086` is enough.

v05.title: bash -x and a safe test
v05.text: Trace every step of the script with `bash -x`; then try `rm` with an empty `DIR` only through `echo` (no real deleting).

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/scripts
bash -x loop.sh 2>&1 | head -8
DIR=""
echo rm -rf $DIR/*
blocks.expected:
+ for i in 1 2 3
+ echo n=1
n=1
...
rm -rf /bin /boot /etc ...

differs: Lines starting with `+` are the `bash -x` trace; several `+` signs mean nested commands.
The last line is only `echo`, so nothing is deleted; it just shows that the empty variable becomes `/*`.

q1.q: What happens with `rm -rf $DIR/*` when `DIR` is empty, and which notation protects?
options: Only the home directory is deleted; use `sudo`
q1.explain: The empty variable disappears and the command becomes `rm -rf /*`. `${DIR:?}` stops the script on an empty value.

q2.q: Which pattern reads a file safely line by line?
options: `while IFS= read -r l; do ... done < file`
q2.explain: `for` with `$(cat)` splits lines into words. `while IFS= read -r` reads the line unchanged.

q3.q: What does `local x=1` do inside a function?
options: Makes `x` valid only inside the function
q3.explain: `local` limits the scope to the function; a variable of the same name outside is left untouched.

options: However the script ends (including errors); except after `kill -9`
Before the first line of the script
q4.explain: The EXIT trap runs on normal exit, on errors and on most signals; SIGKILL cannot be caught.

summary: `for` runs once per list item, `while` as long as the condition is true; choose a safe source.
Read files with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < file`, not with `$(cat)`.
`case ... esac` routes arguments and menus readably; `*)` is the default branch.
Use `local` in functions; walk arrays with `"${arr[@]}"`.
Create temporary files with `mktemp` and clean up with `trap cleanup EXIT`.
Quote every variable; write `"${DIR:?}"` when deleting and test with `echo` first.
`bash -n`, `bash -x` and `shellcheck` show errors without running or step by step.

glossary.meaning: A construct that repeats a block of commands: `for`, `while`.
Splitting an unquoted variable at whitespace.
The characters the shell uses to separate words (field separator).
Multi-way branch that compares a value with patterns.
Keyword that limits a variable to a function.
A Bash variable holding several values under one name.
Defines a command to run on a signal or at exit.
Creates a temporary file or directory with a unique name.
Static analysis tool for shell scripts.
Trace mode that prints every command with its expansions before running it.
